note: Warrant officers, such as the gunner, held rank by warrant, below commissioned officers.
source: W. H. Smyth, The Sailor’s Word-Book (1867), “Warrant-officers”, https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/26000

note: Petty officers were senior sailors with authority over the ordinary crew, below the warrant officers.
source: W. H. Smyth, The Sailor’s Word-Book (1867), “Petty-officers”, https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/26000

note: On a warship the master-at-arms was the petty officer who kept order and acted somewhat like a policeman.
source: W. H. Smyth, The Sailor’s Word-Book (1867), “Master-at-arms”, https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/26000

note: Equivocal: having two meanings, unclear.
A cutlass is a short, heavy curved sword used at sea.

anchor: giving to nitre and sulphur the preeminence over steel
note: Nitre and sulphur are the ingredients of gunpowder, which replaced hand-to-hand fighting with swords.

anchor: a sort of Chief of Police
note: The master-at-arms enforced order below decks, much as a police chief does.
Populous: crowded with people, as the lower gun decks were.

anchor: cleanly cut as those on a Greek medallion
note: A medallion is a large medal or round plaque with a portrait, here with fine, regular features.
Tecumseh was a famous Shawnee leader who led resistance to American expansion in the early 1800s.
Titus Oates (1649 to 1705) invented the Popish Plot of 1678, a false tale of a Catholic conspiracy that led to the execution of innocent people.

anchor: phrenologically associated with more than average intellect
note: Phrenology was a nineteenth-century pseudoscience that claimed the shape of the skull showed a person’s mental powers.

anchor: making a foil to the pallor below
note: Foil: something whose contrast sets off another.

anchor: a pallor tinged with a faint shade of amber
note: Pallor: unhealthy paleness of the skin, here Claggart’s amber tint.
Incog: short for incognito, hiding one’s true identity.
Naturalization: becoming a citizen of a country where one was not born.
Perdue: French for lost, hidden. A secret rumor passed in whispers.

anchor: a chevalier who had volunteered into the King’s Navy
note: Chevalier: a French knight or gentleman, here a man of some rank in disgrace.
Compounding: settling a charge by agreement. The rumor says he joined the navy to escape trial.
Arraigned: formally charged in court. The King’s Bench was a high English court.
Wiseacres: people who claim to be wise but are not.

anchor: the invidious a vague field for unfavorable surmise
note: Invidious: likely to provoke resentment, spiteful. Surmise: a guess.

anchor: press-gangs notoriously abroad both afloat and ashore
note: Press-gangs were parties of sailors sent to seize men for the navy by force. They worked both in ports and at sea.

anchor: at liberty to capture any able-bodied suspect
note: Able-bodied: physically fit and strong enough for service.
Insolvent: unable to pay one’s debts.

anchor: the promiscuous lame ducks of morality
note: Lame ducks: failures who cannot keep up. Promiscuous: of mixed, indiscriminate kinds.

anchor: as much in sanctuary, as the transgressor of the Middle Ages
note: Sanctuary: a place where criminals were safe from arrest, such as a church.

anchor: an old pensioner in a cocked hat with whom I had a most interesting talk on the terrace at Greenwich
note: Greenwich Hospital was a home for old and disabled navy sailors. Its pensioners were a familiar sight.
A man who had fought in Nelson’s great victory in 1805.
Quota: the required number of men for the ship.

anchor: eked out by draughts culled direct from the jails
note: Eked out: stretched to make enough. Draughts: drafts, groups of men chosen and sent. Culled: picked out.

anchor: rose shrieking from the din and dust of the fallen Bastille
note: The Bastille, a royal fortress in Paris, was stormed by the Parisians on 14 July 1789. Its fall began the French Revolution.

anchor: Americans who had fought at Bunker Hill
note: Bunker Hill, near Boston in June 1775, was the first considerable battle of the American War of Independence, fought by men then still living.

anchor: this French upstart from the revolutionary chaos
note: Upstart: a person who has risen suddenly to power. Here Napoleon.
The Apocalypse, or Book of Revelation, foretells terrible judgments before the end of the world.
Quid-nunc: a gossip, from Latin for “what now?”

anchor: the man brokers and land-sharks of the sea-ports
note: Land-sharks: swindlers who preyed on sailors ashore.
source: W. H. Smyth, The Sailor’s Word-Book (1867), “Land-shark”, https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/26000

note: Sobriety: seriousness, soberness. Claggart seems steady and serious.
Ingratiating: trying to win favor.
Ferreting: searching out secrets, as a ferret hunts rabbits.
Austere: stern and strict, without softness or show of feeling.
Ship’s corporals were petty officers who helped the master-at-arms keep order.
source: W. H. Smyth, The Sailor’s Word-Book (1867), “Ship’s corporal”, https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/26000

note: Converging: coming together. The master-at-arms controls hidden channels of influence.
Understrappers: underlings, lowly assistants who do his work.
Commonalty: the common people, here the ordinary crew.
